newsitem.title: INDIA: India strike goes on as truckers consider new offer.
newsitem.headline: India strike goes on as truckers consider new offer.

text.p: India's striking truck owners kept more than two million vehicles off the road for the ninth day on Wednesday while they considered a government offer to solve the crisis, state and transport officials said.
The strike was triggered by a planned five percent service tax on road transport and a sharp rise in insurance premiums, keeping at least 2.2 million trucks stranded.

"The government has proposed a revised formula that truckers will not be responsible to collect the service tax," S.P. Singh, spokesman for the All-India Motor Transport Congress (AIMTC), told Reuters.
"Our national action committee will meet on Wednesday to discuss the legal implications of the government's proposal."

Government officials said they expected to narrow down the the areas of disagreement soon. "Positive negotiations are going on," Yogendra Narain, the highest-ranking civil servant in the Surface Transport Ministry, told Reuters.
AIMTC secretary general Chittranjan Dass said in a statement on Tuesday the government and the truck owners had reached a draft agreement which fell short of the demand to remove the service tax.
The tax was proposed by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram in his federal budget for financial year 1997/98 (April-March).

The coalition government of Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, fighting for its life after the Congress party withdrew its support, has said it cannot rescind the tax because the budget proposals are before parliament.
The budget is being held hostage by the political crisis. Deve Gowda faces a confidence vote on Friday.
"If the budget is not passed, then the whole problem would be solved," Singh said. "But still we have to wait and watch."
The government has offered to refer the rise in insurance premiums to a government panel for consideration.
The bulk of the country's truck fleet is made up of small transporters who own one or two vehicles, but government official Narain said the transport of essential commodities had been satisfactory.
"Prices have certainly not risen substantially," he said. "But the strike has definitely affected industry and ports."
S.V. Damankar, secretary of the Bombay Port Trust, which is among India's busiest ports, said cargo handling had fallen off to 3,000 tonnes per day compared with the usual 250,000 tonnes.
Analysts said businesses which depended on agricultural produce were the worst-hit as movements had been restricted.

"The economy is losing at least 70 billion to 80 billion rupees ($1.9 billion to $2.2 billion) per day," K.R. Vishwanathan, a senior economist at the Birla Economic Research Foundation, told Reuters. ($1 = 35.9 rupees)
